h1:
First Time in Sing Buri
What to Know + Trip Plan
intro: Sing Buri is a small province on the Chao Phraya River, only about 2 hours from Bangkok, so you can see it in a single day's drive. It's known for the heroic history of Bang Rachan, old temples, and riverside food like Mae La fish and boat noodles. If it's your first time and you're not sure where to start, this guide rounds up what to know before you go, plus a 2-day plan you can actually follow.

blocks.html: Plenty of people drive right past Sing Buri on the Asia Highway toward Ayutthaya or Nakhon Sawan without ever stopping, even though the province has more than enough to keep you busy: a giant reclining Buddha, the well-known story of the Bang Rachan heroes, and Chao Phraya riverside food that's hard to find in big cities. Before you set off, here's what a first-timer should sort out.

blocks.text: Where is Sing Buri and how to get there

blocks.html: Sing Buri sits in central Thailand, about 140 km from Bangkok. Driving takes roughly 2 hours along Highway 32 (the Asia Highway) — the same road you take to Ayutthaya and Ang Thong, just a little past Ang Thong. It's the kind of place that's easiest to explore with your own car, since the sights are spread out beyond the town center.

items: Private car — the easiest option. From Bangkok take the Asia Highway (Hwy 32), about 2 hours. Best if you want to hop between districts.
Van / coach — buses leave from Mo Chit and the new Southern terminal and drop you in Sing Buri town, but once you arrive you'll need to hire a local car or motorbike.
Renting a car in Ayutthaya — if you're not driving from Bangkok, plenty of people rent a car in Ayutthaya and drive up from there.

blocks.title: First-timer tip
blocks.html: Sing Buri's main sights are in different districts — Bang Rachan camp and Wat Phikun Thong, for example, are a fair distance from town. If you don't have your own car, plan your route ahead and hire a local driver by the day; it works out cheaper than calling one for each leg.

blocks.html: If it's your first visit and time is tight, these four are the heart of Sing Buri. They cover temples, history, and old-time atmosphere, and you can fit them into 1–2 easy days.

items.name: Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi Worawihan
items.blurb: An old temple in Chakkrasi subdistrict, home to a large reclining Buddha about 47 meters long in Sukhothai style — one of the biggest reclining Buddhas in Thailand. The grounds are shady and pleasant, good for paying respects and taking photos.

items.name: Bang Rachan Heroes Memorial Park
items.blurb: A monument and park telling the story of the Bang Rachan villagers who joined forces against the Burmese in the late Ayutthaya period. There's a heroes' monument, statues, and shady grounds to wander — a landmark most Thais know well.

items.name: Wat Pho Kao Ton + Old Thai Market
items.blurb: A temple tied to the history of Bang Rachan camp. Inside is the Ban Rachan old-style Thai market where you can sample traditional sweets and old-school snacks. It has a vintage-market feel and only opens on certain days, so check before you go.

items.name: Wat Phikun Thong Royal Temple
items.blurb: A temple in Tha Chang district, about 15 km from town, with a large Buddha image and a big Ganesha statue to pay respects to. It's a popular stop for making wishes.

blocks.text: Food you have to try in Sing Buri

blocks.html: Sing Buri sits right on the Chao Phraya River, so its specialties are river food — especially the nationally famous Mae La fish and boat noodles you'll find all over the province. Here's what first-timers shouldn't miss.

items.name: Mae La fish
items.blurb: A freshwater fish from the Mae La stream, known for soft, fatty flesh with no muddy taste. Many roadside spots serve it as grilled Mae La snakehead, tom yum, or chu chee. It's the province's signature dish, and people make the trip just to eat it on the spot.

items.name: Sing Buri boat noodles
items.blurb: Rich, bold-flavored boat noodles found right across the province. They're cheap, so you can eat several bowls, and many famous shops are around the town center and along the Asia Highway.

items.name: Grilled river prawns
items.blurb: Another Chao Phraya riverside favorite. Many waterfront restaurants serve big river prawns grilled or roasted with the prawn fat — great for a bigger meal with a group.

items.name: Thai sweets at the old market
items.blurb: The Ban Rachan old-style Thai market has traditional sweets — thong yip, thong yod, khanom krok — and old-fashioned snacks to nibble as you walk. Good to pick up and take home.

blocks.title: About the food
blocks.html: The well-known Mae La fish and boat noodle shops mostly open from midday into the afternoon, and many close by evening. If you've got your heart set on a famous spot, make it a lunch — don't count on going for dinner.

blocks.text: When's the best time to visit Sing Buri

blocks.html: Sing Buri is fine to visit year-round, but the most comfortable stretch is the cool season, roughly November to February, when it's not hot and you can enjoy the temples and markets. In the rainy season watch out for flooding, since the province sits right on the Chao Phraya and some riverside areas can be affected — if you come then, check flood news first.

items: Nov–Feb — cool and pleasant, great for being outdoors; the best time to come.
Mar–May — hot, so do temples and indoor spots in the late morning and avoid the midday sun.
Jun–Oct — rainy season, lush and green but pack for rain and check the river-water situation along the Chao Phraya.

blocks.text: What first-timers should prep before going

items: Map your route on your phone — the sights are in different districts, so pin them ahead of time so you don't get lost.
Dress modestly for temples — skip spaghetti straps and very short shorts when entering ordination halls and shrines.
Carry cash — many roadside spots and old markets still take mostly cash.
Allow time for lunch — popular spots get crowded, you may queue, and many close in the afternoon.
Fill up the tank — if you're crossing districts, gas stations outside town can be far apart.

faq.q: Is one day enough for Sing Buri?
faq.a: One day is enough for the main highlights — Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi, Bang Rachan camp, and eating Mae La fish — since it's only about 2 hours from Bangkok. But if you want to take it easy and add Wat Phikun Thong and the riverside, an overnight 2-day, 1-night trip is just right.

faq.q: What should I eat in Sing Buri?
faq.a: The signature is Mae La fish, a soft-fleshed freshwater fish from the Mae La stream. Next come Sing Buri boat noodles, found all over the province, and grilled river prawns at the Chao Phraya riverside restaurants.

faq.q: Can I visit Sing Buri without my own car?
faq.a: You can, but it's less convenient than driving, since the sights are spread across different districts. We'd suggest taking a van or coach into town, then hiring a local driver by the day, or renting a car in Ayutthaya and driving up.

faq.q: What makes Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi special?
faq.a: It's an old temple housing a large reclining Buddha about 47 meters long in Sukhothai style — one of the biggest reclining Buddhas in the country and the province's main temple for paying respects.

faq.q: When's the best time to go to Sing Buri?
faq.a: November to February is cool and comfortable, the best stretch for being outdoors. In the rainy season, check the Chao Phraya river-water situation before you travel.
